Factorizations by column blocks and Schubert polynomials as products of key polynomials

Xuanying Han Address: Department of Mathematics, Tianjin University of Finance and Economics, Tianjin 300222, P.R. China Email address: hanxuanying@stu.tjufe.edu.cn , Shunli Ma Address: Department of Mathematics, Tianjin University of Finance and Economics, Tianjin 300222, P.R. China Email address: mashunli@stu.tjufe.edu.cn and Sophie C. C. Sun Address: Department of Mathematics, Tianjin University of Finance and Economics, Tianjin 300222, P.R. China Email address: sophiesun@tjufe.edu.cn
Abstract.

We classify the Schubert polynomials that are products of key polynomials and explicitly determine their finest key factorization. Their indexing permutations are precisely those avoiding ten classical patterns of length six, which form the minimal pattern basis. More generally, the connected components of the column interaction graph give the unique finest factorization of a dual flagged Weyl character into nonconstant diagram characters. Every other such factorization is obtained by grouping these components. We also prove Makhija’s conjecture on products of elementary symmetric polynomials in initial alphabets, allowing repeated alphabets. In this case, the elementary factors are uniquely determined, up to order, by the nonempty Rothe columns.

Key words and phrases: 
Schubert polynomial, key polynomial, column interaction graph, pattern avoidance

1. Introduction

Schubert polynomials represent Schubert classes in the cohomology of flag varieties [4], and each is a nonnegative integer linear combination of key polynomials [13]. A Schubert polynomial is itself a key polynomial exactly when its indexing permutation avoids 21432143; see Reiner and Shimozono [13] and [12, Theorem 3.3]. We ask when a Schubert polynomial is a product of keys and how to determine its finest such factorization.

To study these products, we use dual flagged Weyl characters, which we call diagram characters. For a diagram D=(D1,…,Dm)D=(D_{1},\ldots,D_{m}), where DjD_{j} is the set of occupied rows in column jj, write χD\chi_{D} for its character. Rothe and skyline diagrams give Schubert and key polynomials, respectively [4]. The product of the individual column characters is a coefficientwise upper bound for χD\chi_{D}. Equality in this bound is precisely a factorization into individual column characters. Fan and Guo [3] characterized equality for Schubert and key polynomials; in the Schubert case, it holds exactly when the indexing permutation avoids 14231423 and 14321432. Peng, Lin, and Sun [9, Theorem 1.1] gave the criterion for arbitrary diagrams.

We extend this question from individual columns to blocks of columns. The obstruction to separating two columns is recorded by the column interaction graph ΓD\Gamma_{D}: its vertices are the nonempty indexed columns of DD, and two columns are joined when they share an empty row above a row occupied in both. We prove that the characters of the column blocks multiply to χD\chi_{D} exactly when no edge of ΓD\Gamma_{D} joins different blocks.

It remains to check that column partitions account for all factorizations into diagram characters. Here we use the fact that χD\chi_{D} determines the multiset of nonempty columns of DD, a consequence of [5, Theorem 1.4]. Every factorization into nonconstant diagram characters must therefore come from a column partition. Together with the block criterion, this shows that the connected components give the unique finest factorization, up to order; every other such factorization is obtained by grouping the component factors.11 1 The blocks need not have disjoint row sets; compare the disjoint-row tensor products in [1, Example 1.6]. For factorizations of Ehrhart polynomials of Schubitopes, see Dou, Fan, and Liu [2].

The key-product problem now reduces to recognizing which component characters are keys. A component character is a key polynomial precisely when its columns form a chain under inclusion. For Rothe diagrams, this condition gives the pattern classification below.

To state it, write 𝔖w\mathfrak{S}_{w} for a Schubert polynomial and κα\kappa_{\alpha} for the key indexed by a weak composition α\alpha, a finite sequence of nonnegative integers. All factors use the fixed variables x1,x2,…x_{1},x_{2},\ldots, without relabeling. A key product is a finite product of nonconstant keys; a single factor and the empty product 11 are allowed. For w=w1⋯wn∈Snw=w_{1}\cdots w_{n}\in S_{n}, the Rothe diagram D⁡(w)D(w) has columns Dj​(w)={i:i⁡<w−1​(j),wi>​j}D_{j}(w)=\{i:i<w^{-1}(j),\ w_{i}>j\}. Classical pattern containment means having a subsequence with the same relative order as the pattern. Set

ℬ={\displaystyle\mathcal{B}=\{ 135264,136254,153264,163254,315264,316254,\displaystyle 135264,136254,153264,163254,315264,316254,
142635,142653,143625,143652}.\displaystyle 142635,142653,143625,143652\}. (1.1)
Theorem 1.1.

The Schubert polynomial 𝔖w\mathfrak{S}_{w} is a key product if and only if ww avoids every pattern in ℬ\mathcal{B}. The ten patterns in (1.1) form the minimal classical pattern basis.

For such a permutation, group the nonempty Rothe columns by the connected components of ΓD⁡(w)\Gamma_{D(w)}. Let α(1),…,α(s)\alpha^{(1)},\ldots,\alpha^{(s)} record the numbers of boxes in each row of the resulting subdiagrams. Then the unique finest key factorization, up to order, is

𝔖w=∏t=1sκα(t).\mathfrak{S}_{w}=\prod_{t=1}^{s}\kappa_{\alpha^{(t)}}.

The same column criterion also applies to products of elementary symmetric polynomials. For 1≤b≤a1\leq b\leq a, the polynomial eb​(x1,…,xa)e_{b}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{a}) is the character of the interval column {a−b+1,…,a}\{a-b+1,\ldots,a\}. An elementary product is a finite product of these polynomials, allowing repeated initial alphabets, a single factor, and the empty product 11.

If each initial alphabet is used at most once, the product is a standard elementary monomial. Hatam, Johnson, Liu, and Macaulay [6] gave determinantal formulas for expansions of Schubert polynomials in this basis when the indexing permutation avoids thirteen specified patterns. Woodruff [14, Theorem 4] proved that a Schubert polynomial is a single standard elementary monomial exactly when its permutation avoids 312312 and 14321432. For products allowing repeated initial alphabets, Makhija [11, Section 1.7] conjectured the four-pattern criterion below and gave a pipe-dream argument for sufficiency [11, Section 2]. We prove the converse and determine the factors uniquely.

Theorem 1.2.

The Schubert polynomial 𝔖w\mathfrak{S}_{w} is an elementary product if and only if ww avoids 14231423, 14321432, 31423142, and 41324132, as conjectured by Makhija [11, Section 1.7]. In this case the factorization is unique, up to order, and is

𝔖w=∏Dj​(w)≠∅e|Dj​(w)|​(x1,…,xmax⁡Dj​(w)).\mathfrak{S}_{w}=\prod_{D_{j}(w)\neq\varnothing}e_{|D_{j}(w)|}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{\max D_{j}(w)}). (1.2)

In this case, Proposition 2.1 forces the elementary factors to come from the individual Rothe columns. The criterion for separating these columns [3, 9] and the characterization of interval Rothe columns [10, Proposition 2.3] give the four forbidden patterns. Each interval column determines its elementary factor, which also proves uniqueness.

Section 2 recalls the determinant model and shows that a diagram character determines the multiset of its nonempty columns. Section 3 proves the criterion for column blocks and the finest factorization. Sections 4 and 5 apply these results to key and elementary products, respectively.

2. Columns and diagram characters

All vector spaces are over ℂ\mathbb{C}. We use [N]={1,…,N}[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\} and [a,b]={a,a+1,…,b}[a,b]=\{a,a+1,\ldots,b\}, with NN large enough to contain the rows of every diagram under discussion. For row sets A,BA,B, the difference A∖BA\setminus B consists of the rows belonging to AA but not to BB. Empty columns contribute 11 and play no part in column partitions. Copies of the same nonempty column retain their separate indices.

2.1. Allowed upward moves and column characters

Allowed moves in a column shift its boxes upwards without changing their order. For two row sets of size bb, C={c1<⋯<cb}C=\{c_{1}<\cdots<c_{b}\} and A={a1<⋯<ab}A=\{a_{1}<\cdots<a_{b}\}, we write C⪯AC\preceq A in Gale order if ci≤aic_{i}\leq a_{i} for every ii, and call CC allowed for AA. For diagrams E=(E1,…,Em)E=(E_{1},\ldots,E_{m}) and D=(D1,…,Dm)D=(D_{1},\ldots,D_{m}) with |Ej|=|Dj||E_{j}|=|D_{j}| for every jj, write E⪯DE\preceq D if Ej⪯DjE_{j}\preceq D_{j} for every jj. We record the row counts of EE by the monomial

xE=∏j∏i∈Ejxi.x^{E}=\prod_{j}\prod_{i\in E_{j}}x_{i}.

Thus the exponent of xix_{i} is the number of cells in row ii of EE.

We encode these allowed row choices by minors of a generic upper triangular N×NN\times N matrix Y=(yi​j)Y=(y_{ij}). We write YACY_{A}^{C} for its submatrix with row set CC and column set AA, both in increasing order. For a column AA, the determinants det(YAC)\det(Y_{A}^{C}) with C⪯AC\preceq A are called its allowed minors. For C=AC=A, this is the principal minor det(YAA)\det(Y_{A}^{A}). For a diagram DD, taking one allowed minor from each column gives the products that span the polynomial space

MD=spanℂ⁡{∏jdet(YDjEj):E⪯D}.M_{D}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{C}}\left\{\prod_{j}\det(Y_{D_{j}}^{E_{j}}):E\preceq D\right\}.

We grade by rows, assigning weight xix_{i} to yi​jy_{ij}. The coefficient [xβ]​χD[x^{\beta}]\chi_{D} is the dimension of the part of MDM_{D} having weight xβx^{\beta}.

For a single column,

FA=χ(A)=∑C⪯AxC,xC=∏i∈Cxi.F_{A}=\chi_{(A)}=\sum_{C\preceq A}x^{C},\qquad x^{C}=\prod_{i\in C}x_{i}. (2.1)

For C={c1<⋯<cb}⪯A={a1<⋯<ab}C=\{c_{1}<\cdots<c_{b}\}\preceq A=\{a_{1}<\cdots<a_{b}\}, the minor det(YAC)\det(Y_{A}^{C}) contains ∏iyci,ai\prod_{i}y_{c_{i},a_{i}} with coefficient 11, hence is nonzero. As different CC give different row weights, the allowed minors are independent.

For several columns, the products of allowed minors need not be independent. Since they span MDM_{D}, we obtain the coefficientwise bound

χD≤∏jcoeff⁡FDj=∑E⪯DxE.\chi_{D}\leq_{\mathrm{coeff}}\prod_{j}F_{D_{j}}=\sum_{E\preceq D}x^{E}.

Each product of allowed minors is nonzero, so every monomial on the right also occurs in χD\chi_{D}. Thus the two sides have the same support, although their coefficients may differ.

For D=({2},{2})D=(\{2\},\{2\}), each column has the two allowed minors y12y_{12} and y22y_{22}. Consequently,

MD=spanℂ⁡{y122,y12​y22,y222},χD=x12+x1​x2+x22.M_{D}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{C}}\{y_{12}^{2},y_{12}y_{22},y_{22}^{2}\},\qquad\chi_{D}=x_{1}^{2}+x_{1}x_{2}+x_{2}^{2}.

By contrast, (F{2})2=(x1+x2)2(F_{\{2\}})^{2}=(x_{1}+x_{2})^{2} has coefficient 22 at x1​x2x_{1}x_{2}. The two choices of column minors give the same product y12​y22y_{12}y_{22}, which contributes only once to the character.

For characters with 00–11 coefficients, see Guo, Lin, and Peng [7]. For related bounds on Schubert monomials, see Guo and Lin [8].

Permuting the columns does not change MDM_{D} or χD\chi_{D}. When comparing diagrams, we place them in a common N×NN\times N grid, enlarging NN and adding empty columns if necessary. These operations leave their spaces and characters unchanged.

2.2. Skyline diagrams and key polynomials

For a weak composition α∈ℤ≥0N\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{N}, the skyline diagram Sky⁡(α)\operatorname{Sky}(\alpha) has αi\alpha_{i} left-justified cells in row ii. Its character is κα\kappa_{\alpha}, and κ0=1\kappa_{0}=1. The nonempty columns of Sky⁡(α)\operatorname{Sky}(\alpha) are the sets

{i:αi≥1}⊇{i:αi≥2}⊇⋯.\{i:\alpha_{i}\geq 1\}\supseteq\{i:\alpha_{i}\geq 2\}\supseteq\cdots.

These columns form an inclusion chain, meaning that they are pairwise comparable by inclusion. Conversely, any inclusion chain of columns can be put in skyline order. The number of boxes in each row gives the indexing composition. Figure 1 shows Sky⁡(3,0,2,1)\operatorname{Sky}(3,0,2,1), with column sets {1,3,4}⊇{1,3}⊇{1}\{1,3,4\}\supseteq\{1,3\}\supseteq\{1\}.

For example, κ(1,0)=x1\kappa_{(1,0)}=x_{1} and κ(0,1)=x1+x2\kappa_{(0,1)}=x_{1}+x_{2}. Trailing zeros do not affect a key.

For Rothe diagrams, χD⁡(w)=𝔖w\chi_{D(w)}=\mathfrak{S}_{w}. These identifications use the conventions of [4, 9]. When omitting empty Rothe columns, we keep the original labels of the remaining columns.

2.3. The interaction graph

A pair of rows i<ji<j is a witness for an interaction between AA and BB if row ii is vacant in both columns and row jj is occupied in both.

Only the two witness rows are shown; the columns need not be consecutive in the diagram. A nonempty column [a][a] is isolated in ΓD\Gamma_{D}, since every row above an occupied row is also occupied.

Peng, Lin, and Sun [9, Theorem 1.1] characterized equality in the coefficientwise bound for two columns:

χ(A,B)=FAFB⟺A and B do not interact.\chi_{(A,B)}=F_{A}F_{B}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\text{ and }B\text{ do not interact}. (2.2)

2.4. Column multisets and character factorizations

The following proposition is a direct consequence of Hafner, Mészáros, Setiabrata, and St. Dizier’s Theorem 1.4 [5]. We include a short proof and its application to products of diagram characters.

Proposition 2.1.

On a common [N][N], the monomials occurring in χD\chi_{D} determine the multiset of nonempty columns of DD. In particular, if

χD=χE(1)⋯χE(k),\chi_{D}=\chi_{E^{(1)}}\cdots\chi_{E^{(k)}},

then the nonempty columns of the E(t)E^{(t)} together are exactly the nonempty columns of DD, with multiplicity.

Proof.

For each nonempty A⊆[N]A\subseteq[N], set

rA​(S)=maxC⪯A⁡|C∩S|(S⊆[N]).r_{A}(S)=\max_{C\preceq A}|C\cap S|\qquad(S\subseteq[N]).

This is the maximum number of boxes of AA that can lie in rows of SS after allowed moves. It is the rank function of the Schubert matroid indexed by AA. The functions rAr_{A}, over nonempty A⊆[N]A\subseteq[N], are linearly independent by [5, Theorem 1.4].

Let mD​(A)m_{D}(A) be the multiplicity of a nonempty column AA in DD. Every monomial in χD\chi_{D} is the weight of an allowed choice of rows. For fixed SS, choose a maximizing allowed row set in each column. The resulting product of minors is nonzero, so its weight occurs in χD\chi_{D}. Grouping equal columns gives, for every S⊆[N]S\subseteq[N],

max⁡∑i∈S[xβ]​χD≠0⁡βi\displaystyle\max_{[x^{\beta}]\chi_{D}\neq 0}\sum_{i\in S}\beta_{i} =∑Dj≠∅rDj​(S)\displaystyle=\sum_{D_{j}\neq\varnothing}r_{D_{j}}(S)
=∑∅≠A⊆[N]mD​(A)​rA​(S).\displaystyle=\sum_{\varnothing\neq A\subseteq[N]}m_{D}(A)r_{A}(S).

Linear independence of the functions rAr_{A} therefore determines every multiplicity mD​(A)m_{D}(A).

These maxima add under multiplication of polynomials with nonnegative coefficients. Applying this to the asserted product identity and using linear independence once more gives mD​(A)=∑tmE(t)​(A)m_{D}(A)=\sum_{t}m_{E^{(t)}}(A) for every nonempty AA, as required. ∎

3. Factorization by column blocks

We prove that a partition of the columns gives a factorization exactly when no interaction edge joins different blocks. Together with Proposition 2.1, this yields the unique finest factorization into nonconstant diagram characters, up to order.

3.1. Block factorization

For a set JJ of column indices, write D⁡[J]D[J] for the subdiagram consisting of those columns.

Theorem 3.1.

Let π\pi be a partition of the indices of the nonempty columns of DD. Then

χD≤∏J∈πcoeff⁡χD⁡[J],\chi_{D}\leq_{\mathrm{coeff}}\prod_{J\in\pi}\chi_{D[J]},

with equality precisely when no edge of ΓD\Gamma_{D} joins distinct blocks, or equivalently when each block is a union of connected components. If such an edge exists, at least one coefficient is strictly smaller.

We begin with two blocks. Even if their minors share matrix entries, the evaluations of the two blocks can be prescribed independently when there is no edge between them. It suffices to work with upper unitriangular matrices.

Lemma 3.2.

For every fixed diagram DD, setting yj​j=1y_{jj}=1 for all jj defines an injective linear map on MDM_{D}.

Proof.

Put

dj=#⁡{u:j∈Du}.d_{j}=\#\{u:j\in D_{u}\}.

Every monomial yνy^{\nu} occurring in MDM_{D} has total degree djd_{j} in the variables y1​j,…,yj​jy_{1j},\ldots,y_{jj}. After setting yj​j=1y_{jj}=1, the omitted exponent is still determined by

νj​j=dj−∑i<jνi​j.\nu_{jj}=d_{j}-\sum_{i<j}\nu_{ij}.

Thus two distinct monomials cannot become the same monomial after the substitution. Hence a nonzero element of MDM_{D} remains nonzero after this substitution, proving injectivity. ∎

Lemma 3.3.

Let PP and QQ be two blocks of columns with no interaction edge between them. For any upper unitriangular matrices U,VU,V there is an upper unitriangular matrix WW satisfying

f⁡(W)=f⁡(U)(f∈MP),g⁡(W)=g⁡(V)(g∈MQ).f(W)=f(U)\quad(f\in M_{P}),\qquad g(W)=g(V)\quad(g\in M_{Q}).
Proof.

Set Wj​j=1W_{jj}=1 and Wi​j=0W_{ij}=0 for i>ji>j. For each jj, determine the entries above the diagonal in column jj of WW recursively, in the order i=j−1,j−2,…,1i=j-1,j-2,\ldots,1. We choose each of these entries according to the following rules. If a column of PP contains jj but not i<ji<j, impose

(U−1​W)i​j=0.(U^{-1}W)_{ij}=0.

If the corresponding condition comes from QQ, require (V−1​W)i​j=0(V^{-1}W)_{ij}=0 instead. Both conditions could apply only if columns of PP and QQ contained jj but omitted ii, which would give an interaction edge. If neither condition applies, take Wi​j=0W_{ij}=0. Matrix multiplication gives

(U−1​W)i​j=Wi​j+(U−1)i​j+∑i<ℓ<j(U−1)i​ℓ​Wℓ​j.(U^{-1}W)_{ij}=W_{ij}+(U^{-1})_{ij}+\sum_{i<\ell<j}(U^{-1})_{i\ell}W_{\ell j}.

The coefficient of Wi​jW_{ij} is 11, and the other entries of WW have already been chosen farther down column jj. The same holds with VV in place of UU, so the construction is well defined.

Now fix a column AA in PP and write H=U−1​WH=U^{-1}W. For j∈Aj\in A and i∉Ai\notin A, we have Hi​j=0H_{ij}=0: by triangularity if i>ji>j, and by construction if i<ji<j. The matrix HAAH_{A}^{A} is upper unitriangular. Hence, for every C⪯AC\preceq A,

WAC\displaystyle W_{A}^{C} =UAC​HAA,\displaystyle=U_{A}^{C}H_{A}^{A},
det(WAC)\displaystyle\det(W_{A}^{C}) =det(UAC)​det(HAA)=det(UAC).\displaystyle=\det(U_{A}^{C})\det(H_{A}^{A})=\det(U_{A}^{C}).

Choose one allowed minor for each column of PP. Multiplying the corresponding equalities shows that the resulting product has the same value at WW and UU. These products span MPM_{P}, so f⁡(W)=f⁡(U)f(W)=f(U) for every f∈MPf\in M_{P}. The same argument gives g⁡(W)=g⁡(V)g(W)=g(V) for every g∈MQg\in M_{Q}. ∎

Example 3.4.

Take A={1,3}A=\{1,3\} and B={2,3}B=\{2,3\}. They both contain row 33, but there is no interaction edge between them. For

(1ac01b001),\begin{pmatrix}1&a&c\\ 0&1&b\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix},

the allowed minors are b,1b,1 for AA and a​b−c,a,1ab-c,a,1 for BB. The two sets of minors share the entry bb. Nevertheless, we can prescribe b=μb=\mu for AA and a=λa=\lambda, a​b−c=ρab-c=\rho for BB by taking c=λ​μ−ρc=\lambda\mu-\rho. For example, μ=2\mu=2, λ=3\lambda=3, and ρ=5\rho=5 give c=1c=1.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

The claim is immediate for a single block. For two blocks P,QP,Q, choose homogeneous bases f1,…,frf_{1},\ldots,f_{r} of MPM_{P} and g1,…,gsg_{1},\ldots,g_{s} of MQM_{Q}. Their pairwise products span MDM_{D}. In each row degree, the coefficient of χP​χQ\chi_{P}\chi_{Q} counts the corresponding pairs (i,j)(i,j), whereas the coefficient of χD\chi_{D} is the dimension of the span of their products. It follows that

χD≤coeffχPχQ.\chi_{D}\leq_{\mathrm{coeff}}\chi_{P}\chi_{Q}. (3.1)

Equality holds if and only if the products fi​gjf_{i}g_{j} are linearly independent.

Suppose there is no edge from PP to QQ, and consider a linear relation

∑i=1r∑j=1sci​j​fi​(W)​gj​(W)=0\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{s}c_{ij}f_{i}(W)g_{j}(W)=0

holding identically for upper triangular matrices WW. For arbitrary upper unitriangular matrices U,VU,V, apply this identity to a matrix WW supplied by Lemma 3.3, with fi​(W)=fi​(U)f_{i}(W)=f_{i}(U) and gj​(W)=gj​(V)g_{j}(W)=g_{j}(V) for all i,ji,j. This gives

∑i=1r∑j=1sci​j​fi​(U)​gj​(V)=0.\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{s}c_{ij}f_{i}(U)g_{j}(V)=0.

By Lemma 3.2, both bases remain linearly independent on upper unitriangular matrices. Fixing VV and varying UU therefore gives ∑j=1sci​j​gj​(V)=0\sum_{j=1}^{s}c_{ij}g_{j}(V)=0 for every ii. The independence of the gjg_{j}, as VV varies, then gives ci​j=0c_{ij}=0 for all i,ji,j. The products fi​gjf_{i}g_{j} are therefore linearly independent, so equality holds in (3.1).

Conversely, suppose that a column AA of PP interacts with a column BB of QQ. By (2.2), there is a nontrivial homogeneous linear relation among products of an allowed minor of AA and an allowed minor of BB.

For every indexed column other than the chosen columns AA and BB, fix its principal minor. Multiply each allowed minor of AA by the fixed minors from PP, and each allowed minor of BB by those from QQ. The resulting families lie in MPM_{P} and MQM_{Q}, respectively. They consist of homogeneous polynomials and are linearly independent: the allowed minors of each column are independent, and multiplication by a fixed nonzero polynomial preserves this property. Extend these families to homogeneous bases of MPM_{P} and MQM_{Q}.

Multiplying the original relation by all the fixed minors gives a nontrivial relation among products indexed by distinct pairs of basis elements. Hence equality in (3.1) is impossible, and the inequality is strict in at least one row degree.

For more than two blocks, iterate this result. Without crossing edges every split gives equality. Otherwise, let PP consist of the columns in a block of π\pi containing one endpoint of a crossing edge, and let QQ consist of the columns in the other blocks. The first split is strict. Applying the same inequality within QQ gives

χD<coeffχPχQ≤coeff∏J∈πχD⁡[J].\chi_{D}<_{\mathrm{coeff}}\chi_{P}\chi_{Q}\leq_{\mathrm{coeff}}\prod_{J\in\pi}\chi_{D[J]}.

Here <coeff<_{\mathrm{coeff}} means coefficientwise inequality with strict inequality in at least one coefficient. The description in terms of connected components follows. ∎

3.2. The finest factorization

Recall that a factorization is finer than another when the latter is obtained by grouping factors of the former.

Corollary 3.5.

Let K1,…,KsK_{1},\ldots,K_{s} be the connected components of ΓD\Gamma_{D}. By Proposition 2.1 and Theorem 3.1, the factorizations of χD\chi_{D} into nonconstant diagram characters are precisely those obtained by grouping these components. Hence

χD=∏t=1sχD⁡[Kt]\chi_{D}=\prod_{t=1}^{s}\chi_{D[K_{t}]}

is the unique finest such factorization, up to order.

Example 3.6.

For the columns A,BA,B in Example 3.4, take D=(A,A,B,B)D=(A,A,B,B), as shown in Figure 2. The two copies of AA interact, as do the two copies of BB, but no AA interacts with a BB. The dashed rounded boxes mark the two components, with column indices {1,2}\{1,2\} and {3,4}\{3,4\}. The component factorization is

χD=χ(A,A)​χ(B,B),\chi_{D}=\chi_{(A,A)}\chi_{(B,B)},

where

χ(A,A)=x12​(x22+x2​x3+x32),χ(B,B)=s(2,2)​(x1,x2,x3).\chi_{(A,A)}=x_{1}^{2}(x_{2}^{2}+x_{2}x_{3}+x_{3}^{2}),\qquad\chi_{(B,B)}=s_{(2,2)}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}).

Here s(2,2)s_{(2,2)} is the Schur polynomial. Since each component contains an edge, neither factor splits further into the characters of its two columns.

4. Products of key polynomials

We apply the criterion for factorization by column blocks to key products. We first characterize the components whose characters are single key polynomials, and then translate the component condition for Rothe diagrams into pattern avoidance.

4.1. The column condition

We begin with the criterion for a single key polynomial.

Remark 4.1.

A diagram character χE\chi_{E} is a key polynomial if and only if its nonempty columns form an inclusion chain. Indeed, the columns of a chain can be arranged as a skyline, and the converse follows from Proposition 2.1. The indexing composition α\alpha is given by the row counts of EE, so χE=κα\chi_{E}=\kappa_{\alpha}.

Example 4.2.

A key polynomial can factor further. Let D=Sky⁡(2,0,1)D=\operatorname{Sky}(2,0,1). Its columns are D1={1,3}D_{1}=\{1,3\} and D2={1}D_{2}=\{1\}. They satisfy D1⊋D2D_{1}\supsetneq D_{2} but do not interact. In Figure 3, the two dashed rounded boxes mark the singleton components, and the inclusion sign compares the two row sets. Hence

κ(2,0,1)=x12​(x2+x3)=κ(1)​κ(1,0,1).\kappa_{(2,0,1)}=x_{1}^{2}(x_{2}+x_{3})=\kappa_{(1)}\kappa_{(1,0,1)}.
Theorem 4.3.

The character χD\chi_{D} is a key product if and only if the columns in every connected component of ΓD\Gamma_{D} form an inclusion chain. When this holds, let K1,…,KsK_{1},\ldots,K_{s} be these components, and let αi(t)\alpha_{i}^{(t)} count the boxes in row ii of D⁡[Kt]D[K_{t}]. Then

χD=∏t=1sκα(t).\chi_{D}=\prod_{t=1}^{s}\kappa_{\alpha^{(t)}}.

This is the unique finest key factorization, up to order; indexing compositions are understood up to trailing zero parts.

Proof.

A key factor is a skyline character, so its columns form an inclusion chain by Remark 4.1. Proposition 2.1 and Corollary 3.5 show that a connected component cannot be split among different factors. Thus every component must be a chain. Conversely, when the components are chains, arrange the columns of each as a skyline. Their characters are the claimed keys, and the component factorization is the unique finest one. ∎

4.2. The pattern condition

Even if every edge joins comparable columns, the columns in a connected component need not form an inclusion chain. Consider w=142635w=142635, whose nonempty Rothe columns are

D2={2},D3={2,4},D5={4}.D_{2}=\{2\},\qquad D_{3}=\{2,4\},\qquad D_{5}=\{4\}.

Figure 4 shows the path D2−D3−D5D_{2}-D_{3}-D_{5}. The dashed rounded box encloses its single component. Its neighboring columns satisfy D2⊊D3⊋D5D_{2}\subsetneq D_{3}\supsetneq D_{5}, but the endpoints are incomparable.

Lemma 4.4.

Every component of ΓD\Gamma_{D} whose columns do not form an inclusion chain contains either an edge between incomparable columns, or a path A−B−CA-B-C with incomparable endpoints and

B⊆A∩CorB⊇A∪C.B\subseteq A\cap C\qquad\text{or}\qquad B\supseteq A\cup C.
Proof.

Choose incomparable columns A,CA,C having minimum graph distance in their component and take a shortest path between them. Distance one gives the first alternative. Otherwise, every other pair of vertices on the path has smaller graph distance than A,CA,C and is therefore comparable by minimality. In particular, the internal columns form a chain, and each is comparable with both AA and CC. If an internal column BB satisfied A⊆B⊆CA\subseteq B\subseteq C or C⊆B⊆AC\subseteq B\subseteq A, then A,CA,C would be comparable, a contradiction. Thus every internal column is either contained in both endpoints or contains both.

These two types cannot both occur. Indeed, consecutive internal columns of different types would give L⊆A∩CL\subseteq A\cap C and H⊇A∪CH\supseteq A\cup C with an edge L​HLH. A row pair witnessing this edge is vacant in HH and occupied in LL, hence vacant and occupied, respectively, in both AA and CC. This would make A,CA,C adjacent.

If the internal columns are all contained in A∩CA\cap C, choose the largest one, BB. Since B⊆A∩CB\subseteq A\cap C, the row pair witnessing the first edge of the path also witnesses A​BAB; the last edge similarly witnesses B​CBC. If all internal columns contain A∪CA\cup C, choose the smallest one instead. The same reasoning, with inclusions reversed, gives A​BAB and B​CBC. ∎

A diagram is northwest if boxes at the northeast and southwest corners of a rectangle force a box at the northwest corner. Equivalently, when AA lies to the left of CC, every row of C∖AC\setminus A is below every row of AA.

Lemma 4.5.

Let DD be a northwest diagram. A component of ΓD\Gamma_{D} fails to be an inclusion chain if and only if it contains either an edge between incomparable columns, or a path of length two A−B−CA-B-C with nonadjacent incomparable endpoints and

B⊇A∪C.B\supseteq A\cup C.
Proof.

By Lemma 4.4, it suffices to exclude B⊆A∩CB\subseteq A\cap C when the incomparable endpoints are nonadjacent. Put AA to the left of CC, and let i<ji<j witness A​BAB. Then j∈B⊆Cj\in B\subseteq C, whereas i∉Ai\notin A. If ii were in CC, it would belong to C∖AC\setminus A above the box at row jj of AA, contrary to the northwest property. Thus i∉Ci\notin C as well. The same pair i<ji<j witnesses A​CAC, so the endpoints cannot be nonadjacent. ∎

Remark 4.6.

Rothe diagrams are northwest. For j<kj<k, every row in Dk​(w)∖Dj​(w)D_{k}(w)\setminus D_{j}(w) lies below row w−1​(j)w^{-1}(j), while every row of Dj​(w)D_{j}(w) lies above it. Consequently, the components of ΓD⁡(w)\Gamma_{D(w)} satisfy the characterization in Lemma 4.5.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

The factorization formula and its uniqueness follow from Theorem 4.3. It remains to prove the avoidance criterion and minimality.

Suppose 𝔖w\mathfrak{S}_{w} is not a key product. By Theorem 4.3 and Remark 4.6, there are incomparable Rothe columns Dj,DkD_{j},D_{k}, j<kj<k, joined either by an edge or by a path of length two through a column containing both. In each case, we find a subsequence of ww whose pattern lies in ℬ\mathcal{B}.

Choose entries x,yx,y with w−1​(x)∈Dj∖Dkw^{-1}(x)\in D_{j}\setminus D_{k} and w−1​(y)∈Dk∖Djw^{-1}(y)\in D_{k}\setminus D_{j}. Then x>jx>j and y>ky>k, with xx preceding jj and yy preceding kk. Since y>k>jy>k>j but w−1​(y)∉Djw^{-1}(y)\notin D_{j}, yy follows jj; hence xx precedes kk and, since w−1​(x)∉Dkw^{-1}(x)\notin D_{k}, satisfies x<kx<k. Thus four selected entries occur as

x​j​y​k,j<x<k<y.x\,j\,y\,k,\qquad j<x<k<y.

Since w−1​(v)∈Dj∩Dkw^{-1}(v)\in D_{j}\cap D_{k}, the entry vv is larger than kk and precedes both jj and kk. The entry uu precedes vv, and hence jj. Since w−1​(u)∉Djw^{-1}(u)\notin D_{j}, the definition of a Rothe column gives u<ju<j. Thus u<j<k<vu<j<k<v. In particular,

u<j<x<k<min⁡(v,y).u<j<x<k<\min(v,y).

5. Products of elementary symmetric polynomials

The polynomial eb​(x1,…,xa)e_{b}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{a}) is the sum of the squarefree monomials of degree bb in x1,…,xax_{1},\ldots,x_{a}. Since the factors have nonnegative coefficients, no variable appearing in a factor can disappear from the product. We may therefore work in a common finite alphabet.

Lemma 5.1.

For 1≤b≤a1\leq b\leq a,

F[a−b+1,a]=eb​(x1,…,xa).F_{[a-b+1,a]}=e_{b}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{a}).

Conversely, if FA=eb​(x1,…,xa)F_{A}=e_{b}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{a}) with A≠∅A\neq\varnothing, then A=[a−b+1,a]A=[a-b+1,a].

Proof.

If C={c1<⋯<cb}⊆[a]C=\{c_{1}<\cdots<c_{b}\}\subseteq[a], then ci≤a−b+ic_{i}\leq a-b+i. Hence the allowed row sets for [a−b+1,a][a-b+1,a] are precisely the subsets of [a][a] of size bb. Formula (2.1) gives the identity.

Conversely, equality forces the degrees and supports to agree. Their greatest row sets in Gale order are AA and [a−b+1,a][a-b+1,a], respectively, so these sets are equal. ∎

Proposition 5.2.

The character χD\chi_{D} is an elementary product if and only if every nonempty column of DD is an interval and ΓD\Gamma_{D} is edgeless.

Proof.

By Lemma 5.1, every elementary factor is the character of an interval column. If their product is χD\chi_{D}, Proposition 2.1 shows that the interval columns, with multiplicities, are exactly the nonempty columns of DD. Thus χD=∏Dj≠∅FDj\chi_{D}=\prod_{D_{j}\neq\varnothing}F_{D_{j}}. Applying Theorem 3.1 to the partition into singleton column blocks shows that ΓD\Gamma_{D} is edgeless.

Conversely, if ΓD\Gamma_{D} is edgeless, Theorem 3.1 gives χD=∏Dj≠∅FDj\chi_{D}=\prod_{D_{j}\neq\varnothing}F_{D_{j}}. By Lemma 5.1, these factors are elementary when the columns are intervals. ∎

Lemma 5.3.

For w∈Snw\in S_{n}, the graph ΓD⁡(w)\Gamma_{D(w)} is edgeless if and only if ww avoids 14231423 and 14321432, and every nonempty column of D⁡(w)D(w) is an interval if and only if ww avoids 31423142 and 41324132.

Proof.

Suppose Dj,DkD_{j},D_{k} interact, with j<kj<k. By the definition of the Rothe columns, a witness consists of rows w−1​(u)<w−1​(v)w^{-1}(u)<w^{-1}(v), where the entries u,vu,v occur before j,kj,k and satisfy u<j<k<vu<j<k<v. Depending on which of j,kj,k occurs first, the selected entries form 14231423 or 14321432. Conversely, either pattern provides just such a witness.

For the interval condition, suppose that a nonempty column DjD_{j} is not an interval. It then has a gap, a vacant row between two occupied rows. Let u,v,zu,v,z be the entries of ww in these rows, from top to bottom. By the definition of DjD_{j}, the occupied rows lie above row w−1​(j)w^{-1}(j) and contain values larger than jj, while the intervening vacant row contains a value smaller than jj. Hence w−1​(u)<w−1​(v)<w−1​(z)<w−1​(j)w^{-1}(u)<w^{-1}(v)<w^{-1}(z)<w^{-1}(j) and v<j<min⁡(u,z)v<j<\min(u,z). The selected entries occur as u​v​z​ju\,v\,z\,j, giving pattern 31423142 or 41324132 according to whether u<zu<z or z<uz<u. Either pattern conversely gives a gap in the column indexed by the last selected entry. ∎

The edgeless condition is equivalent to the equality criterion of Fan and Guo [3]. The characterization using interval columns is due to Liu, Mészáros, and St. Dizier [10, Proposition 2.3].

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Proposition 5.2 and Lemma 5.3 give the avoidance criterion. The factors are those in (1.2) by Lemma 5.1. By Proposition 2.1, the interval columns are determined with multiplicities. Each such column AA fixes b=|A|b=|A| and a=max⁡Aa=\max A, so the factorization is unique up to order. ∎

Figure 5 shows the Rothe diagrams for 24312431, 14231423, and 31423142, from left to right. They illustrate an elementary product and the two obstructions in Proposition 5.2. The dashed boxes group the nonempty column labels by connected component; labels of empty columns remain unboxed. For w=2431w=2431, the nonempty Rothe columns are

D1=[1,3],D3={2}.D_{1}=[1,3],\qquad D_{3}=\{2\}.

These intervals do not interact, giving

𝔖2431=e3​(x1,x2,x3)​e1​(x1,x2).\mathfrak{S}_{2431}=e_{3}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})e_{1}(x_{1},x_{2}).

For 14231423, the two nonempty columns are both {2}\{2\}, so they interact:

𝔖1423=x12+x1​x2+x22≠(x1+x2)2.\mathfrak{S}_{1423}=x_{1}^{2}+x_{1}x_{2}+x_{2}^{2}\neq(x_{1}+x_{2})^{2}.

For 31423142, the graph is edgeless, but D2={1,3}D_{2}=\{1,3\} is not an interval.

Allowing repeated initial alphabets matters. A standard elementary monomial (SEM) has the form

∏i≥1eai​(x1,…,xi),0≤ai≤i,\prod_{i\geq 1}e_{a_{i}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{i}),\qquad 0\leq a_{i}\leq i,

where e0=1e_{0}=1 and all but finitely many aia_{i} vanish. Woodruff [14, Definition 2 and Theorem 4] characterized single-SEM Schubert polynomials by avoidance of 312312 and 14321432. In contrast, 𝔖312=x12=e1​(x1)2\mathfrak{S}_{312}=x_{1}^{2}=e_{1}(x_{1})^{2} is an elementary product that uses the alphabet {x1}\{x_{1}\} twice.
